an0852.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low? Running a blended Meta + Google mix for my eyewear brand, last 30 days I got 710K impressions, 6,732 clicks so CTR is around 0.9%. Feels low. Targeting is broad / interest-based. How do I get the CTR up?
an0852.assistant: You're staring at the wrong number. A 0.9% CTR on broad, interest-based traffic is honestly unremarkable — fixing it gets you more clicks, and more clicks is not your problem. Look one step down: 6,732 clicks turned into 58 orders. That's a 0.86% conversion rate. People are clicking and then leaving without buying, which tells you the traffic isn't low-quality at the top — it's low-intent. Broad/interest targeting finds people who'll click a nice pair of frames out of curiosity, not people who decided this week they need new glasses. At ₹2,050 AOV, eyewear is a considered purchase; browsers don't convert. Chasing CTR just buys you more browsers. The lever: shift from interest-based to high-intent — on Google, exact and phrase-match keywords like 'buy blue light glasses online', layered with negatives to kill the freebie/information traffic; on Meta, lean on retargeting and lookalikes off actual purchasers rather than cold interest stacks. Stop optimising campaigns for clicks and optimise for purchases. One caveat: 58 orders in 30 days is a thin sample to draw hard conclusions from per audience — give the high-intent setup two to three weeks before you judge whether intent was really the lever.

an0853.user: Need a sharp pair of eyes on this. Flipkart seller, Google Search, last 30 days post-iOS. Spend ₹14.5L. an0853.assistant: Nothing's 'wrong' — you're refereeing a fight that has no winner. Both numbers are biased in opposite directions and neither is the truth. The platform's 4.3 is modelled conversions on a 7-day-click window — it over-counts, claiming credit for sales that would have happened anyway and ones it merely touched. Shopify last-click at 1.6 is the opposite — it hands all the credit to the final click and strips it from the ad that actually created the demand, especially brutal post-iOS when view-through is invisible. The real ROAS sits somewhere between 1.6 and 4.3, and no amount of squinting at either dashboard will pin it. The trap is picking the flattering one (4.3) or panicking on the scary one (1.6). Both are vanity in different costumes. Anchor on something neither platform can spin: blended CAC. Total spend ÷ actual new customers from your Shopify backend — that's ₹14.5L divided by your real net-new buyers this month. Manage to that single number against your contribution per order; if blended CAC sits under contribution, you're fine regardless of what either ROAS claims. Caveat: 'new customers' has to mean first-time buyers, not total orders — if you blend in repeat purchasers you'll flatter your CAC and be right back to lying to yourself, just with a third number.

an0854.user: Flipkart seller, running Meta. Pasting last 30 days, tell me what's wrong: 50,000 visits, 3,206 add to cart, 2,239 reached checkout, 656 purchases. CTR on the ads is 2.3%. Something's bleeding and I can't see it.
an0854.assistant: Walk the funnel and the leak points to itself. 50,000 visits → 3,206 add-to-cart is a 6% ATC rate — healthy; your ads and product page are doing their job. 3,206 → 2,239 reaching checkout is a normal drop. Then 2,239 reached checkout → 656 purchases. That's 29%. Roughly seven in ten people who pull out their wallet and start checkout walk away before paying. A working checkout converts 50-70% from that step. The leak isn't acquisition — it's the very last metre, and that's almost always friction you can't see from the ad dashboard: a shipping charge that appears only at the final screen, a forced account creation, no UPI or COD option, a coupon field that screams 'go hunt for a code', or a payment gateway timing out. The lever: instrument the checkout and fix it. Don't touch the ad spend — pouring more traffic in just feeds a leakier bucket. Go through your own checkout on a cheap Android phone over mobile data and watch where it makes you hesitate; that's where the 71% is dying. Caveat: confirm the gap is genuine drop-off and not legit COD/abandonment that later converts via your recovery flow — pull the actual checkout-abandonment reasons before you assume it's all pure friction.

an0855.user: Want your read on this before I do something rash. D2C coffee, Meesho Ads. CTR dropped 13% week-over-week and I'm honestly about to tear up the whole strategy and rebuild. We did 94 conversions this week. Is the creative dead?
an0855.assistant: Do nothing. Genuinely — close the tab. A 13% CTR swing on a week with 94 conversions isn't a trend, it's noise. On a base that small, a single slow Tuesday, a festive-week dip, or a couple of weaker placements will move CTR more than that, and it'll bounce back next week with no action from you. Overhauling your whole strategy off one wobbly week is exactly how founders whipsaw their accounts into the ground — every reset throws the algorithm back into learning and torches the next two weeks too. The creative isn't dead; you don't have enough data to claim it's even sick. What would actually count as a signal: the same direction holding for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a swing big enough in a single week to clearly clear normal variance — a 30-40%+ drop, not 13%. Until then there's no decision to make. Caveat: if you'd seen frequency climbing and CTR sliding together over a month, that's real creative fatigue worth acting on — but you're looking at one week, and one week tells you nothing.

an0859.user: Calm question, looking for the non-obvious angle. D2C haircare on YouTube, last 30 days: AOV ₹750, gross margin 31%, CAC ₹441, ROAS sitting at 1.7, CTR 2.1%. My main question is just — how do I lower my CAC?

You lose roughly ₹208 on every single order before you've done anything wrong on the ad side. Even if you were brilliant and cut CAC by a fifth — ₹441 down to ₹353 — you'd still be at ₹232.50 − ₹353 = −₹120.50, still underwater. The disease isn't your CAC; it's a 31% gross margin. At that margin each sale only generates ₹232.50 to cover the entire cost of acquiring it, and no targeting tweak, no creative test, no audience tightening can close a ₹208 hole. You're asking a marketing question about a unit-economics problem. The lever: leave the ads alone and fix the margin — get COGS down with better sourcing or pack sizing, raise price, or lift AOV with bundles/subscription so the contribution turns positive. You need gross margin into the 50%+ range or AOV well north of ₹750 before ROAS even deserves your attention. Caveat: if there's strong repeat purchase you're not counting here, LTV could rescue it — but on a single 30-day first-order view, this is margin, not marketing.
